title: Private Equity: Your Ears Will Bleed
summary: Josh and Chuck explain private equity: what it is, how leveraged buyouts work, the "two and twenty" fee structure, and the history from Milton Friedman and Michael Jensen through KKR's early deals, RJR Nabisco, and the 1980s corporate raiders. They walk through case studies of Toys R Us, Sears/Kmart under Edward Lampert, and Red Lobster, then cover private equity in newspapers, healthcare, dental practices, nursing homes, housing (Blackstone), and the positive example of Hilton. They close with the carried interest tax loophole, pension fund exposure, and a listener email about a grandmother who paid for family dinners.

segments.title: Opening and framing private equity
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode on private equity and gives a basic definition: a private fund that buys controlling interests or whole companies, streamlines them, and sells for profit. Chuck adds that it is a riskier, less transparent alternative investment.

segments.title: Transparency and accredited investors
segments.summary: The hosts explain that private equity is less regulated than stocks and bonds, and that investors must be accredited, meaning either sophisticated or wealthy, usually institutions like large funds or college endowments.

segments.title: Two and twenty fees and managers' profits
segments.summary: Managing partners earn the two and twenty formula: two percent of total assets plus twenty percent of profits above a threshold. Josh notes that fees are kept even when the company fails or workers are laid off.

segments.title: Leveraged buyouts explained
segments.summary: Chuck explains that most deals are leveraged buyouts, financed by a loan the target company must repay. Josh offers a house-mortgage analogy.

segments.title: Milton Friedman and the shareholder doctrine
segments.summary: Private equity's scale today is described, with about thirteen million US employees and about two trillion dollars. The hosts credit Milton Friedman's argument that a corporation's only job is to serve shareholders.

segments.title: Michael Jensen and CEO stock pay
segments.summary: Josh credits Harvard economist Michael Jensen with aligning CEOs with shareholders through stock pay and with using debt to force lean management.

segments.title: Breaking companies apart and Wall Street
segments.summary: Chuck describes breaking companies up and selling assets as tactics. The hosts reference the movie Wall Street and its airline storyline.

segments.title: Sale-leaseback and dividend recapitalizations
segments.summary: Private equity sells company real estate and leases it back at higher rates. Josh uses Red Lobster as an example and describes taking new loans to pay investors. The hosts note some firms do save companies.

segments.title: Short-term flipping
segments.summary: Chuck describes the house-flip model of buying companies to make them look healthy for resale.

segments.title: Customers suffer under private equity
segments.summary: Josh says product and service quality usually suffers as buyers cut costs and charge more.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with banter about Anacott Steel shirt and Danny's sweater.

segments.title: Early history: KKR and Houdaille
segments.summary: Chuck covers the post-World War Two origins of leveraged buyouts, with Jerome Kohlberg, Henry Kravis and George Roberts forming KKR. Their first big deal was Houdaille Industries in 1979, bought for about 380 million dollars with about a million paid up front. Josh says the company was run into the ground.

segments.title: RJR Nabisco and the 1980s raiders
segments.summary: Chuck describes the RJR Nabisco buyout, covered in Barbarians at the Gate and its film adaptation. Josh says about two thousand jobs were lost and that the 1980s corporate raiders became outlaw figures. Firms such as Bain Capital, Blackstone and Carlyle were founded in the 1980s.

segments.title: Post-crash regulation and growth
segments.summary: Chuck says private equity largely weathered the 2008 crash and that Congress added some reporting requirements. Public companies have fallen by about half since 1996, and by 2023 there were five times as many private equity-backed firms as public companies.

segments.title: Toys R Us takeover
segments.summary: Josh says a private equity takeover ran Toys R Us into the ground, with about thirty thousand jobs lost.

segments.title: Sears and Kmart under Edward Lampert
segments.summary: Kmart went bankrupt in 2002 and Edward Lampert's hedge fund ESL became the largest shareholder and chairman. Kmart bought Sears to form Sears Holdings. The hosts describe a six billion dollar stock buyback that starved the business of capital expenditure, and ESL lending about 2.6 billion dollars to the company. In 2015 Lampert founded Seritage Growth Properties, which bought Sears and Kmart buildings and leased them back.

segments.title: Sears bankruptcy and store closures
segments.summary: Josh says the sale-leaseback was legal but unfair. Sears Holdings filed for bankruptcy after about seven years, closing stores from about 3,500 to around 800 by the time of the episode. The company had about eleven billion dollars in unpaid debt, and Lampert personally made about 1.4 billion dollars. The Wall Street Journal estimated about 200,000 jobs lost.

segments.title: Red Lobster buyout and shrimp promotion
segments.summary: In 2014 Golden Gate Capital bought Red Lobster for 2.1 billion dollars and sold the real estate of about 500 restaurants for about 1.5 billion, which was leased back at above-market rates. Chuck and Josh joke about Josh's time as a server at Red Lobster. During COVID, Thai Union Group became the exclusive shrimp supplier and pushed endless shrimp for twenty dollars, losing about eleven million dollars in three months.

segments.title: Niche firms and Roark Capital
segments.summary: Josh says some firms focus on specific industries, like Roark Capital in fast food, which lobbied to remove the fifteen dollar federal minimum wage from a stimulus package. Chuck notes the firm's name comes from Howard Roark in The Fountainhead.

segments.title: Private equity and newspapers
segments.summary: Chuck says private equity ownership of newspapers rose from about 5 percent in 2001 to 23 percent in 2019, with staff cuts and declining local election participation. Josh adds that the loss of local news has had broad effects. The hosts also mention Great Value's valuation drop from about six billion in 2017 to 350 million in 2023.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Private equity in healthcare and dental
segments.summary: Chuck cites 166 healthcare leveraged buyouts in 2024 and seven of the eight biggest healthcare bankruptcies that year. Josh describes dental practices owned by private equity, with an Ohio case of a three-year-old allegedly told to get seven root canals. Hospitals owned by private equity face higher charges and complications, and a study links private equity ownership to an eleven percent increase in mortality in hospices and nursing homes.

segments.title: Private equity and nursing home experience
segments.summary: Chuck shares a personal account of a relative's experience in a nursing home and calls the industry horrific.

segments.title: Housing, Blackstone and Hilton success
segments.summary: Blackstone is described as the largest US landlord with about 300,000 rental units in 2023, with rents rising and maintenance slowing. The hosts then describe Blackstone's 2007 Hilton buyout, where CEO Christopher Nassetta invested in digital strategies and emerging markets. Blackstone sold back to the public market in 2013 and exited in 2018 with about 14 billion dollars in profit.

segments.title: Burger King and 3G Capital
segments.summary: Josh says Brazilian firm 3G Capital made about 28 billion dollars over fourteen years on about one billion invested in Burger King.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break and banter.

segments.title: Pension funds, 401k access and carried interest
segments.summary: Chuck notes that eighty-nine percent of public pension funds hold some private equity, averaging about 13 percent of assets. Josh says 401(k) plans can now include private equity, though it is not recommended for non-experts. He explains the carried interest loophole: fund managers pay about 20 percent capital gains tax instead of ordinary income rates, so a hundred million dollars would be taxed about seventeen million less. The hosts say their view is biased.

segments.title: Listener email about grandmother paying for dinner
segments.summary: Chuck reads an email from James about his grandmother Sheila, who repeatedly paid for family dinners, including a case where she called the restaurant from Massachusetts to put the bill on her card. Josh responds and invites more listener mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and close the episode with the standard iHeartRadio credit.
